newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey threatens to strike Cyprus missiles.
newsitem.headline: Turkey threatens to strike Cyprus missiles.

text.p: Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller said on Friday that Turkey would strike in the future at Cyprus's missile systems if the government there went ahead with a plan to deploy them on the divided island.
"These offensive missiles will definitely not be deployed. If they are deployed we will do what is needed, if that means they need to be hit they will be hit," Ciller told a news conference.
Piling the pressure on Cyprus, Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said that if the missile deployment went ahead, he would integrate a disputed no-man's-land into the Turkish sector of the island.

He threatened to take over Varosha, a Turkish-held resort just south of Famagusta that has been closed off since the island was divided in 1974. Most of the property in the resort is owned by Greek Cypriots.

"We will take all measures we see as necessary as long as the decision to buy the S-300 missile systems and as long as the Greek Cypriots insist on continuing with the behaviour that is deepening the confidence crisis on the island," Denktash said.

Turkey has accused the Cypriot government of trying to change the balance of forces on the island by a deal announced over the weekend to buy Russian anti-aircraft missiles that could neutralise Turkish air superiority.

There are 30,000 Turkish troops in the northern third of Cyprus while the internationally recognised Cyprus government controls the Greek Cypriot south. The island has been divided since 1974, when Turkish troops invaded in response to a coup engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.

The United States has urged Nicosia to cancel the Russian missile deal and is to send an envoy to the island over the weekend to try and reduce the tension. Washington estimates the system will not be deployed for at least 16 months.
Reacting to Denktash's comments on Varosha, the United Nations made clear its opposition to any attempt to change the status of the area.
"There was an agreement that this area should remain uninhabited," United Nations spokesman Waldemar Rokoszewski in the Cypriot capital Nicosia told Reuters.
"The secretary general maintains and stresses it holds the government of Turkey responsible for the maintenance of the status quo in the area," he said.
But United Nations efforts to monitor the status quo in the fenced-in area of the town is "extremely limited", he said.
"We are exposed to a tough regime of the Turkish army there."
